stem.text: The function \( f \) is twice differentiable on the open interval \( -4 < x < 7 \). Its derivative \( f' \) is increasing on \( -4 < x < -2 \), decreasing on \( -2 < x < 1 \), and increasing on \( 1 < x < 7 \). On this interval the only zeros of \( f' \) are at \( x = -3 \), \( x = 0 \), and \( x = 3 \). The graph of \( f' \) has a horizontal tangent line at \( x = 5 \), where \( f'(5) = 2 \).

parts.prompt: Find all values of \( x \) in the open interval \( -4 < x < 7 \) at which the graph of \( f \) has a point of inflection. Give a reason for your answer.

worked_solution.text: f' changes from increasing to decreasing at x = -2.
f' changes from decreasing to increasing at x = 1.

points.criterion: Gives exactly x = -2 and x = 1. Listing any other value, such as a zero of f' (-3, 0, 3) or x = 5, does not earn the point.

States that f' changes from increasing to decreasing at x = -2 and from decreasing to increasing at x = 1, or that f' has a relative maximum at x = -2 and a relative minimum at x = 1. A reason given only as f changing concavity or f'' changing sign does not earn the point, and a response that declares an extra value does not earn it.

parts.prompt: Does the graph of \( f \) have a point of inflection at \( x = 5 \)? Give a reason for your answer.

worked_solution.text: f' is increasing on 1 < x < 7, so it is increasing on both sides of x = 5 even though its graph is flat there.

points.criterion: Answers no: the graph of f does not have a point of inflection at x = 5.

States that f' is increasing on both sides of x = 5 (it is increasing on all of 1 < x < 7), so f' does not change from increasing to decreasing or the reverse there; a horizontal tangent of f' alone is not enough. Saying only that f''(5) = 0 does not earn the point.

parts.prompt: Let \( g(x) = \displaystyle\int_{0}^{x} f(t)\,dt \) for \( -4 < x < 7 \). Find all values of \( x \) in \( -4 < x < 7 \) at which the graph of \( g \) has a point of inflection, and determine whether the graph of \( g \) has a point of inflection at \( x = -2 \). Give reasons for your answers.
parts.answer_latex: x = -3, \ x = 0, \ x = 3; \ \text{no inflection at } x = -2

worked_solution.text: By the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus g' = f, so g'' = f'.
f' is increasing through its zero at -3, decreasing through its zero at 0, and increasing through its zero at 3, so it changes sign at each.
f' is increasing to its zero at -3 and decreasing to its zero at 0, so it is positive on both sides of x = -2.

points.criterion: Gives exactly x = -3, x = 0, and x = 3. Including x = -2, x = 1, or x = 5 does not earn the point.
States that g'' = f' (or that the slope of g', which is f, changes sign) and that f' changes sign at x = -3, x = 0, and x = 3. A reason in terms of g changing concavity alone does not earn the point.
States that the graph of g has no point of inflection at x = -2 because g'' = f' is positive on both sides of x = -2 (f' > 0 on -3 < x < 0), so it does not change sign there.

parts.prompt: Let \( k(x) = f(2x) \) for \( 0 < x < \frac{7}{2} \). Find the \( x \)-coordinate of each point of inflection of the graph of \( k \). Give a reason for your answer.

worked_solution.text: By the chain rule k' is 2 f'(2x), so k' increases or decreases exactly as f' does at 2x.
On 0 < x < 7/2 the input 2x runs over 0 < 2x < 7, where f' changes from decreasing to increasing only at 2x = 1.

points.criterion: Gives x = 1/2 (or 0.5) as the only point of inflection of k. Listing x = -1, x = 1, or x = 5/2 as well does not earn the point.

States that k'(x) = 2f'(2x) changes from decreasing to increasing at x = 1/2 because f' changes from decreasing to increasing at 2x = 1, or equivalently that f' has a relative minimum at 1 so k' has one at 1/2.
